questions.scenario: An engineer proposes using the account root user for daily deployments because it always has enough permissions. What is the correct response?

options.text: Use root only for tasks that require it and protect it with MFA.
Create an access key for root and store it in CI.
Share the root password with the platform team.
Use root for deployments but rotate it weekly.

questions.explanation: The root user is reserved for exceptional account-level tasks. Daily work should use federated identities and roles. Learn more in [IAM best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html).

questions.scenario: Employees need browser and CLI access to several AWS accounts using the company identity provider. Which starting point avoids separate long-lived IAM users?

options.text: One IAM user copied into every account.
IAM Identity Center with federated workforce access.
An EC2 instance profile for each employee.
A public S3 bucket containing credentials.

questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center is the recommended path for centralized workforce access across accounts. Learn more in [IAM best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html).

questions.scenario: An ECS task running in private subnets must read one production secret from Secrets Manager. The platform team will rotate the secret and refuses to distribute long-lived IAM user keys through images, task definitions, or environment variables. How should the task receive AWS credentials?

options.text: Bake an access key into the container image.
Pass a shared user key through an environment variable.
Assign a task role with the required permission.
Use the account root access key.

questions.explanation: AWS compute services deliver temporary role credentials to workloads. The task role should contain only the needed permission. Learn more in [IAM best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html).

questions.scenario: An identity policy allows s3:GetObject, but an applicable SCP explicitly denies it. What is the result?

options.text: Allow wins because it is closer to the user.
The policies cancel and AWS asks for MFA.
The bucket becomes public.
The request is denied because explicit deny overrides allow.

questions.explanation: AWS authorization requires an applicable allow and no applicable explicit deny. Learn more in [IAM policy evaluation logic](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html).

questions.scenario: A new AWS organization is defining the identity controls every workload account must adopt. Which controls belong in a sound IAM baseline?

options.text: MFA for privileged human access.
One administrator policy for every application to reduce complexity.
Temporary role credentials for workloads.
Grant AdministratorAccess to every workload to avoid authorization failures.
Regular removal of unused permissions and credentials.

questions.explanation: MFA, temporary credentials, and continuous least-privilege review reduce credential and authorization risk. Learn more in [IAM best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html).
